name: Paeonol

lead: Paeonol is a small phenolic molecule from peony root bark, long used in traditional Chinese medicine.
In skincare circles it is discussed as a plant-derived option for brightening and reducing pigmentation, and it also appears in research for anti-inflammatory effects.

paras: Paeonol is reported to be anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and weakly active on MAO enzymes; in lab studies it has been explored for effects on pigment-producing pathways.
Human data are limited. A phase 2 trial of a paeonol-containing combination was run in knee osteoarthritis. As with any botanical-derived topical, individual sensitivity can vary.

chain: Aimed at a more even, brighter complexion
angle.text: Paeonol is explored as a plant-derived ingredient for reducing pigmentation, and some skincare products include it for tone-evening. Published research summarized here concerns its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties.

lead: Paeonol is a phenolic compound found in peony root bark (moutan cortex) and some other plants, used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine. In the pigment category it is of interest as a plant-derived compound that people explore for skin tone evening and melanin reduction.[1][2]

Published research on paeonol covers anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, cardiovascular and neurological effects, mostly in cells and animals.[3][4][5] A fixed-dose combination of apocynin and paeonol has been tested in a phase 2 knee osteoarthritis trial.[6]
infobox: Peony root bark, Arisaema erubescens, Dioscorea japonica

paras: Paeonol is an O-methylated phenol with a molar mass near 166 g/mol, found in Paeonia suffruticosa and other plants.[1]

A randomized placebo-controlled phase 2 trial tested a fixed-dose apocynin and paeonol combination in symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.[6] A Korean herbal formula containing related ingredients was tested in elderly people with dry mouth.[7] A trial of a compound paeonol dripping pill examined inflammatory mediators in unstable angina.[8] Human urinary metabolites of paeonol have been characterized.[9] Other work is laboratory-based, including reviews of effects on atherosclerosis, the nervous system and cancer.[3][4][5]
